props.title: For Black Folks, Voting Is Not an Option. It’s Mandatory.
props.dek: Our vote is our voice. People bled for the ballot, and the fight did not end in 1965.

props.body:
## Our Vote Is Our Voice: Why Voting Matters So Much to African Americans

Every election season, someone says, “My vote doesn’t really count.” I want to gently push back on that, because for African Americans, the ballot was never a small thing. People bled for it. People died for it. Treating it casually dishonors that sacrifice.

## The Promise That Was Broken

After the Civil War, the 15th Amendment was ratified in 1870, declaring that the right to vote could not be denied because of race. On paper, Black men had won the ballot. In practice, the promise was snatched away almost as fast as it was made.

Across the South, states built an entire machinery designed to keep Black citizens away from the polls:

- Poll taxes that charged a fee to vote, which many Black families, newly freed and often locked out of fair wages, simply could not pay.
- Literacy tests that were rigged. A white applicant might be asked to read a single line, while a Black college graduate was asked to interpret obscure sections of a state constitution.
- Grandfather clauses that exempted men from these tests if their grandfathers had voted before the Civil War, which shut out the formerly enslaved and their descendants.
- White primaries that barred Black voters from the only elections that mattered in one-party states.
- Intimidation and violence, including firings, evictions, beatings, and murders of those who dared to register.

For nearly a century, this was the reality. Black citizens in Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and beyond were taxed, drafted, and governed by leaders they were not allowed to help choose.

## The Struggle That Changed the Law

Ordinary people refused to accept it. Organizers with SNCC, the NAACP, and the SCLC went door to door in the most dangerous counties in America. Fannie Lou Hamer was beaten in a jail cell for trying to register. Medgar Evers was assassinated in his driveway. Three young civil rights workers were murdered in Mississippi during Freedom Summer in 1964.

The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed segregation in public places and employment discrimination, and the 24th Amendment ended poll taxes in federal elections. But the heart of the voting fight was still ahead.

On March 7, 1965, John Lewis and hundreds of peaceful marchers crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, and were met with billy clubs and tear gas. The nation watched on television. That day became known as Bloody Sunday, and it pushed Congress to act. On August 6, 1965, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act, which outlawed discriminatory voting practices and required federal oversight in places with a history of suppression.

The results were dramatic. Black voter registration in the South soared, and Black elected officials began to appear in places where it had been unthinkable.

## The Fight Is Not Over

**Here is the part we cannot forget:** the work did not end in 1965. In 2013, the Supreme Court’s decision in Shelby County v. Holder removed the requirement that certain states get federal approval before changing their voting rules. Since then, debates over voter ID laws, polling place closures, early voting limits, and district maps have continued to shape who can vote easily and who faces obstacles.

You can disagree about policy and still recognize this truth: rights that were won through struggle have to be protected through participation.

## Politics Touches Everything

Some people say they are “not into politics.” But politics is into you, whether you are paying attention or not. Here is where it shows up in everyday life:

**Taxes:** Politicians decide how much you pay, who gets breaks, and where the money goes. Your paycheck, your property tax bill, and your small business all feel those decisions.

**Education:** School funding, teacher pay, class sizes, curriculum, school discipline policies, student loan rules, and school board decisions are all shaped by elected officials. If you have a child in a classroom, politics is already in the room.

**Infrastructure:** The roads you drive, the bridges you cross, the water coming out of your tap, the broadband in your neighborhood, and the bus line you rely on all depend on who gets funded and who gets ignored. Communities that vote consistently tend to get attention. Communities that stay home often get left behind.

**Laws and justice:** Lawmakers decide what is a crime, how it is punished, how policing works, and how courts operate. Prosecutors, sheriffs, and judges, many of them elected, shape what justice looks like in your community.

**Healthcare, housing, and jobs:** Insurance access, minimum wage, rent protections, zoning, and small business support all trace back to decisions made by people we elect.

**Local elections:** The mayor, city council, school board, and county commissioners often affect your daily life more directly than anyone in Washington, and turnout in those races is usually painfully low. Your single vote carries the most weight right there.

## What Voting Really Means

When we vote, we honor the people who marched, the people who were turned away, and the people who never got the chance. We also claim a seat at the table where decisions about our children, our neighborhoods, and our futures are made.

If we do not show up, those decisions get made anyway. They just get made without us.

## Your Next Steps

- Check your registration and make sure it is current.
- Know your voting options, including early voting, mail ballots, and Election Day locations.
- Research every race, not just the top of the ticket.
- Bring someone with you. A neighbor, a coworker, a church member, a first-time voter.
- Talk about it with your family, especially the young people who are watching what we do.

They fought like it mattered because it did.!! Let’s vote like it still does!!
